lesson.title: Cluster Sampling: Picking Whole Groups, Not Individuals
lesson.summary: A cluster sample randomly selects entire pre-existing groups from the population, then includes everyone within the selected clusters, trading some statistical precision for practicality and cost savings.
lesson.body:
A simple random sample, where every individual in the population has an equal chance of being personally selected, is the gold standard for representativeness, but it is not always practical. Imagine trying to survey students across a school district by drawing individual names from a district-wide list of 40,000 students; researchers would need contact information for every one of them and might end up interviewing one or two students scattered across dozens of different schools. Cluster sampling solves this practicality problem differently: instead of randomly selecting individuals, it randomly selects whole, naturally occurring groups, called clusters, and then studies everyone, or almost everyone, inside the selected clusters.

In the school example, the clusters might be entire classrooms or entire schools. A researcher could randomly select 8 classrooms out of the district's 400 classrooms and survey every single student in those 8 classrooms. This requires far less travel and far less administrative setup than tracking down individually scattered names, because once a cluster is chosen, everyone in it is reachable through one visit. The key requirement for this to work well statistically is that each cluster should itself look roughly like a small-scale version of the whole population, containing a similar mix of the traits being studied.

Cluster sampling is easy to confuse with stratified sampling, but the two are opposites in an important sense. A stratified sample divides the population into groups, strata, and then samples from every single stratum, guaranteeing that every group is represented in the final sample. A cluster sample also divides the population into groups, clusters, but then randomly selects only some of those clusters and ignores the rest entirely, hoping that the selected clusters stand in for the ones left out. This is why cluster sampling works best when clusters are heterogeneous internally but similar to one another overall, while stratified sampling is chosen when the opposite is true, when the strata differ meaningfully from each other but are internally uniform.

Consider a hypothetical example. A city wants to estimate average household recycling participation across its 60 neighborhoods, each with roughly similar economic and demographic makeup. Surveying every household in all 60 neighborhoods would be expensive, so the city instead randomly selects 6 neighborhoods and surveys every household within those 6. If the neighborhoods really are similar to one another in composition, this cluster sample can give a reasonably accurate citywide estimate at a fraction of the cost of a full simple random sample, because fieldworkers only need to cover 6 concentrated areas rather than scattered addresses across the entire city.

The tradeoff is precision. Because an entire cluster is included or excluded as a unit, an unusual cluster, one neighborhood that happens to have an unusually high or low recycling rate for reasons unrelated to the rest of the city, can swing the sample's estimate more than a single unusual individual would in a simple random sample. Cluster sampling is chosen deliberately as a practical compromise: it sacrifices some of the statistical precision of a full simple random sample in exchange for a large reduction in cost and logistical burden, and it remains valid as long as the clusters are randomly selected and are reasonably representative of the broader population.
